sections.section_title: Clinical Approach to Multiphasic Anaphylaxis: Case-Based Introduction
sections.description: Uses the presented case of clarithromycin-triggered anaphylaxis with multiple relapses to illustrate rapid recognition, initial stabilization, escalation of care, and disposition decisions in the ED and ICU.
key_points: Recognize anaphylaxis clinically: acute onset of illness with skin/mucosal involvement plus respiratory compromise and/or hypotension, or isolated hypotension/respiratory compromise after likely allergen exposure.
Do not delay intramuscular epinephrine for IV placement or diagnostics; administer 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) in the anterolateral thigh and repeat every 5–15 minutes as needed.
Provide supplemental oxygen, place patient supine with legs elevated (if tolerated), establish IV access, and give rapid isotonic crystalloid boluses for hypotension.
Early involvement of critical care is appropriate when there is hypotension, hypoxemia, airway threat, need for multiple epinephrine doses, or recurrent episodes.
In recurrent (biphasic/multiphasic) episodes, maintain a low threshold for ICU monitoring and consider transition to an epinephrine infusion if repeated IM dosing is required.
Document the suspected trigger (first exposure to clarithromycin), timing, treatments and responses, and adverse medication effects.
Initiate discharge planning only after a sustained symptom-free observation window appropriate to risk, provision of epinephrine auto-injectors, and education.

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology and Definitions: From Single-Episode to Multiphasic Anaphylaxis
sections.description: Explains mast cell/basophil activation and mediator release, mechanistic bases for biphasic/multiphasic reactions, and standard terminology to distinguish clinical patterns.
key_points: Anaphylaxis results from rapid mast cell and basophil degranulation (IgE-mediated in most cases), releasing histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, platelet-activating factor, and cytokines.
Biphasic anaphylaxis: recurrence of symptoms after apparent resolution without re-exposure; typically within 24 hours but reported up to 72+ hours.
Multiphasic anaphylaxis: more than one recurrence (two or more distinct relapses) after initial resolution.
Refractory anaphylaxis: persistent symptoms/signs despite appropriately dosed and administered epinephrine and supportive care.
Potential mechanisms for biphasic/multiphasic courses include delayed secondary mediator synthesis, continued or delayed allergen absorption, or underlying mast cell disorders that amplify responses.
Systemic mastocytosis and other clonal mast cell disorders increase mast cell burden and mediator release, predisposing to severe and possibly multiphasic reactions.

sections.description: Differentiates biphasic/multiphasic anaphylaxis from sustained or refractory anaphylaxis and from common mimics, ensuring accurate classification and tailored management.
key_points: Differentiate true biphasic/multiphasic reactions from sustained anaphylaxis due to ongoing allergen absorption (eg, slow-release medications, retained stingers, depot injections) or inadequate initial epinephrine dosing.
Distinguish refractory anaphylaxis (persistent, not fully responsive) from separated relapses after an asymptomatic interval.

Consider mimics: acute asthma or COPD exacerbation, panic attacks, vasovagal syncope, sepsis, cardiogenic shock, scombroid poisoning, carcinoid syndrome, hereditary angioedema (bradykinin-mediated, minimal urticaria), ACE inhibitor–induced angioedema, and vocal cord dysfunction.
Clinical clues favoring anaphylaxis include urticaria/flushing, pruritus, hypotension or distributive shock physiology, bronchospasm, and response to epinephrine.
Medication-related nuances: macrolide allergy is uncommon but possible; cross-reactivity across macrolides is uncertain—avoidance of the implicated agent and careful documentation are prudent.

sections.description: Outlines targeted testing during and after anaphylaxis, optimal serum tryptase sampling, evaluation for mast cell disorders, and factors that influence observation and admission decisions.
key_points: Serum tryptase confirms mast cell activation but a normal value does not exclude anaphylaxis (especially with food triggers).

Timing for tryptase: obtain as soon as feasible without delaying treatment, again at 1–2 hours (within 4 hours) after symptom onset when levels peak, and a baseline level at least 24 hours after complete clinical resolution.
Interpretation: an acute level exceeding baseline by ≥20% + 2 ng/mL supports mast cell activation (20% + 2 rule).

Evaluate for underlying mast cell disorders when reactions are severe, recurrent, or baseline tryptase is elevated: testing may include KIT D816V mutation analysis, flow cytometry for aberrant mast cell markers (eg, CD25/CD2), bone marrow biopsy, and assessment for WHO criteria.
Remember alternate causes of elevated baseline tryptase (eg, hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, chronic kidney disease, myeloid neoplasms, obesity).

Suggested predictors of biphasic risk include delayed epinephrine administration, severe initial presentation, need for multiple epinephrine doses, and prior biphasic reactions; however, reliable prediction models are lacking.

Observation strategy: use risk stratification—short observation for low-risk (rapid, complete response to a single epinephrine dose, reliable support), 6–12 hours for intermediate risk, and admission/ICU monitoring for severe cases, multiphasic courses, or those needing repeated epinephrine.

sections.section_title: Management: Acute Treatment, Recurrent Episodes, and Disposition
sections.description: Provides a stepwise algorithm for initial and ongoing treatment, including epinephrine dosing, when to use infusions, adjunct therapies, steroid considerations, and discharge planning.
key_points: Epinephrine is first-line and life-saving: 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) IM into the mid-outer thigh; repeat every 5–15 minutes as needed.
Avoid underdosing in adults >50 kg; many auto-injectors contain 0.3 mg—drawn-up 1 mg/mL (1:1000) epinephrine to deliver 0.5 mg IM may be appropriate in healthcare settings.
Establish early IV access and give aggressive isotonic fluids for hypotension; administer high-flow oxygen; monitor continuously (ECG, pulse oximetry, frequent BP).
For bronchospasm, add inhaled beta-2 agonists; consider nebulized epinephrine for upper airway edema.

If multiple IM doses are required or shock persists, initiate a titrated IV epinephrine infusion with ICU-level monitoring; add vasopressors (eg, norepinephrine) in distributive shock unresponsive to epinephrine and fluids.
In patients on beta-blockers with refractory hypotension/bronchospasm, give glucagon (eg, 1–2 mg IV bolus followed by infusion) while continuing epinephrine and fluids.
Antihistamines (H1 ± H2) and corticosteroids are adjuncts for cutaneous symptoms; they do not treat airway or shock and should never delay epinephrine.

Routine corticosteroids to prevent biphasic reactions are not supported by current evidence and may be harmful; limit to specific indications (eg, refractory asthma component) with awareness of risks (hyperglycemia, mood changes).

Consider source control to reduce ongoing allergen absorption (eg, remove insect stinger, stop culprit medication); decontamination is rarely applicable but may be considered early for certain oral exposures if safe.
Disposition: determine observation length based on severity and risk; admit or observe longer for recurrent episodes, severe initial features, or comorbidities; ensure readiness for safe discharge.

At discharge: prescribe and teach use of 2 epinephrine auto-injectors (dose matched to weight), provide a written emergency action plan, arrange allergy follow-up, and document/communicate the suspected trigger and avoidance strategies.

sections.section_title: Clinical Pearls, Pitfalls, and Systems Considerations
sections.description: Summarizes high-yield lessons from the case and evidence base, emphasizing dosing accuracy, monitoring, laboratory timing, and safety systems that reduce morbidity.
key_points: Do not wait for rash or hypotension—treat the clinical syndrome when anaphylaxis is suspected.
Under-dosing epinephrine is common; adults ≥50 kg generally require 0.5 mg IM. Stock pathways for rapid preparation of correct doses when 0.5 mg auto-injectors are unavailable.
Consider epinephrine infusion early in recurrent or refractory cases; avoid repeated delays between IM doses.
Ensure accurate tryptase sampling: acute sample(s) within 1–2 hours of onset and a baseline after full clinical resolution; use the 20% + 2 rule to support diagnosis.
Normal tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis; clinical judgment prevails.
Suspect mast cell disorders when baseline tryptase is elevated or reactions are severe/recurrent; coordinate hematology/allergy evaluation.
Observation should be individualized; severe initial features or need for multiple epinephrine doses warrant prolonged monitoring or admission.
Avoid routine corticosteroids for prevention of biphasic reactions; prioritize epinephrine, oxygen, and fluids.
Address practical factors that affect efficacy: IM site (mid-outer thigh), needle length in obesity, avoiding subcutaneous injection, and rapid access to resuscitation equipment.
Provide comprehensive discharge education: trigger avoidance, early epinephrine use, calling emergency services after self-injection, and carrying two devices at all times.
